北京时间 2026-11-25 最重要的变化是：具身智能的可信度与部署效率开始被同时审视——评估从“任务成功”细化到物理目标达成与接口粒度，推理系统则出现面向 VLA 的通信感知剪枝、潜世界动作模型压缩与专用 kernel 融合。以下按证据强度分级梳理。

**1. WorldLeague：把“物理目标达成”变成可比较的实验**
- 标题/日期/类型/URL：*WorldLeague: Benchmarking Physical Agency*，2026-11-22，arXiv/HF 论文全文摘录，https://huggingface.co/papers/2611.30989
- 旧问题：机器人基准常以 household activities 为单位，掩盖了成功所需的能力组合；不同模型家族（VLM/VLA/WAM）缺乏统一的物理结果比较。
- 机制：60 个模拟任务被分为 WorldSeek（导航/目标 grounding）、WorldShape（几何重配置/物理推理）、WorldShift（时间记忆/约束管理）。不要求统一控制接口：VLM 通过 decision-preserving motion 抽象选择目标与参数，VLA/WAM 使用自身控制。评分基于轨迹是否满足物理谓词，给出 Interactive Score（部分进展）和 physical success rate。
- 差别：与 BEHAVIOR-1K、LIBERO 相比，它把任务按物理挑战分类，并用同一个目标同时比较三类模型，而不是比较固定接口。
- 可信程度：论文全文 HTML 截取，作者报告 Claude Fable 5.2 最高 Interactive Score 28.58/100、13/60 物理成功；VLM 在 QA 全对时 71.8% 的片段 Interactive Score 为零。实验数据为作者自述，尚未独立复现。
- 启示：对 VLA 推理与服务，这提醒不能把 VLM 的视觉问答正确率当作控制能力；闭环轨迹校验成本高，但必须纳入评估。异步控制中，物理进展需要逐步打点，推理系统应支持逐步状态上传而非单次问答。

**2. RUIBench：机器人使用接口（RUI）是重要变量**
- 标题/日期/类型/URL：*RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?*，2026-11-22，arXiv/HF 论文全文摘录，https://huggingface.co/papers/2611.31115
- 旧问题：VLM 控制机器人时，接口决定了 agent 需要命令什么动作、何时获得反馈，但已有基准固定接口，无法分离影响。
- 机制：RUIKit 交叉 6 种 action abstraction（低层运动、图像点、语义技能、程序等）与 2 种 interaction form（per-action 与 program），得到 13 个接口，共享感知与控制。发现改变仅 RUI 会让 frontier agent 成功率从 45% 升到 81%，4B 模型从 13% 到 47%；有效接口减少不必要决策、保留必要反馈。还发现“verification gap”——agent 经常声称成功但物理失败。
- 差别：与 WorldLeague 关注能力不同，这里控制变量是接口，比较决策压缩与程序内反馈。
- 可信程度：HTML 全文含 30 个任务、650 条真机数据描述。数字为作者自述，未见仓库；属论文实验，需独立验证。
- 启示：对 VLA 推理系统，支持 programmatic multi-step action 能显著降低调用频率与 token 开销；但验证必须独立于 VLA 输出，不能信任 agent 的完成声明。异步调度时，需要独立任务级验证器触发重计划。

**3. ComVLA：语言引导的通信感知 VLA 拆分推理**
- 标题/日期/类型/URL：*ComVLA: Communication-Aware Split Inference for VLA Models in 6G-Connected Robotics*，2026-11-25，arXiv cs.RO HTML 全文，https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07838
- 旧问题：VLA 太大无法上端侧，云端推理需传输视觉特征，无线链路带宽受限；语义通信 codec 需针对信道重训练，token pruner 固定预算、不看信道。
- 机制：edge 端用文本指令 embedding 对视觉 token 做 cross-attention，形成 task-aware 表示，再用 dot-product 硬投票给每个视觉 token 重要性打分；根据 Shannon 链路容量估计计算当前可传 token 上限 K*，只传 top-K* 个视觉 token 到云端 VLA。无新增可训练参数。
- 差别：与 LightVLA/VLA-ADP 的固定 token 计数不同，预算随 SNR/带宽动态变化；形式化成受约束互信息的 top-K 选择，操作性强。
- 可信程度：论文 HTML 全文含算法和结果；作者报告在 LIBERO 上传 32 vs 512 tokens，计算省 74%、延迟降 22%，成功率 95.4% vs 96.9%。但配置需核验，未提供代码。
- 启示：证明视觉 token 稀疏性可由任务语言先验在线提取，且带宽与计算能协同调度。VLA serving 系统未来可以把 token budget 作为 QoS 维度，在多客户端间按信道/算力动态分配；异步控制中，上行 token 数可随控制步长和信道状态实时调整。

**4. LeanWAM：把冻结视频模型的先验蒸馏成轻量策略**
- 标题/日期/类型/URL：*LeanWAM: Learning Latent World Action Models from Frozen Video Models*，2026-11-25，arXiv cs.RO HTML 全文，https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31740
- 旧问题：WAM 常在部署时保留大 video generator，训练/推理成本高；不清楚策略究竟需要哪些未来表示、能压多紧。
- 机制：probe 研究发现互补未来特征（Wan VAE latents + DINOv3 features + 联合训练后的 video features）可压缩到 32 甚至 1 个 token 就保留大部分 action-decoding。据此采用两阶段训练：Stage 1 用 Future Extractor 把 transition 压成 32 个 predictive token 作为冻结 video generator 的条件，并从其 hidden states 经 attentive pooler 提取 world tokens；Stage 2 把这两种表示蒸馏到一个 1.4B MoE-Transformer 策略，部署时不再运行 video generator。
- 差别：与 DreamZero、Motus 等保留 video backbone 不同，是先学习可微分压缩代码，再蒸馏到独立策略；比单纯的 feature distillation 更显式利用未来预测监督。
- 可信程度：HTML 全文含 probe 与策略实验；作者报告 A100 上 25.1 ms/action chunk，比代表性 WAM 快 12.3–41.5×。但未独立复现。
- 启示：对 VLA 推理系统，teacher 离线压缩/蒸馏是一条可落地的轻量化路径，25 ms 级别延迟允许更高控制频率或多客户端复用。异步控制中，action chunk 长度与推理延迟的权衡可以重新设计，因为模型本身更快。

**5. RoboDojo-Mirror：镜子让策略失败，且不只是碰撞**
- 标题/日期/类型/URL：*Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies*，2026-11-25，arXiv cs.RO HTML 全文，https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33010
- 旧问题：视觉鲁棒性基准通常扰动视角/光照/背景，但没有覆盖反射表面造成的结构化视觉歧义——目标内容被复制到不可操作位置。
- 机制：在 RoboDojo 上增加无镜、单镜、双镜、镜面桌面四种条件，保持任务目标/成功判据/策略权重一致。用几何匹配的非反射面板作为障碍控制，区分反射与物理碰撞。分析轨迹/接触，发现 50–88% 镜像特定失败无接触，伴随“phantom targeting”反射物和真实目标空间错位；真机 π0.5/FastWAM 同样下降。
- 差别：不是问“模型是否认识镜子”，而是测量闭环操作在反射环境下是否仍能完成；控制组隔离物理障碍因素。
- 可信程度：HTML 全文含协议与结果，作者报告聚合成功率下降 10.8–56.7pp、镜面桌面最多 62.5pp；代码仓库在摘要中给出但未核验。
- 启示：VLA 推理链路必须加入空间一致性/深度过滤或多视角校验，防止 phantom target 触发无效动作和额外控制周期。对多客户端 VLA 服务，非接触性失败意味着即使推理低延迟，任务也可能因视觉歧义反复触发重规划，需要失败检测与成功验证分离。

**6. vLLM GDN prefill kernel 融合：减少 HBM 往返**
- 标题/日期/类型/URL：*[vllm-project/vllm PR] [Perf][Kernel][GDN] Fuse the prefill causal conv1d + post-conv prep into one CUDA kernel*，2026-11-25，GitHub PR 正文，https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/69135
- 旧问题：Qwen3-Next 等 GDN 模型 prefill 中 causal conv1d 与 post-conv prep 是两个 kernel，conv 输出需通过 HBM 往返，长序列时带宽瓶颈明显。
- 机制：把两个算子融合为单一 CUDA kernel，避免中间结果写回；头数在运行时传入，仅 chunk size 是模板参数；sm_103a 使用 packed FP32，其他架构回退标量 FMA。支持 beta_scale，非 SiLU 等保留旧路径。
- 差别：不是替换算子库，而是针对 GDN prefill 的序列结构消除中间 HBM 传输，最小 HBM traffic 从约 1.65 TB/s 提到 5.29 TB/s（32K tokens）。
- 可信程度：PR 自报 kernel 微基准与 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 e2e 提升 2.0% prefill throughput，pytest 28 项通过；尚未合并/外部审核，属 release/PR body。
- 启示：VLA action expert 常含 flow-matching/Diffusion 或 SSM 结构，中间表示若反复落 HBM 会显著抬高推理延迟。这种运行时参数化、融合消除中间写的思路，可迁移到 VLA prefill/action expert kernel 设计，尤其对长观测序列 batch。

**跨领域弱信号**
- *Sparks of Weight-Space Programming*（https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31715，摘要仅）：用语言模型直接读写 π0.5 约 0.0002% 参数，在已微调任务上修正重复失败，无需数据/训练。可信度低（摘要），但若成立，意味着 VLA 出错可通过在线权重编辑解决，绕开重训练。
- *Kimi K3.1 DCP ShardQ*（https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/66027）：稀疏 MLA 在 decode context parallelism 下让 prefill token 跳过 query all-gather/LSE combine，TTFT 108k tokens 1.385× 加速，展示分布式注意力路径如何与稀疏索引协同。

**趋势假设**
1. **RUI 将成为具身评估的一等公民变量，且可被系统化配置**（置信度中高）。可反证实验：若在不同未见任务/机器人上重复 RUIBench，RUI 效果缩小或不稳定，则假设削弱。
2. **VLA 服务化将把 token/带宽/控制率纳入同一优化函数**（置信度中）。ComVLA 表明 token 稀疏性与成功率可折衷，LeanWAM 表明紧凑表示可离线蒸馏。可反证：在真实无线信道或不同 VLA 上，若 token 剪枝导致成功率非线性崩塌，则需放宽假设。
3. **结构化视觉歧义（反射/透明/遮挡）需要独立于物理接触的验证滤波器**（置信度中）。RoboDojo-Mirror 中大量无接触失败提示深度/空间一致性检查可缓解。可反证：若仅通过多视角深度补全或反射数据增强就能恢复到基线，则问题归为感知而非控制链路。

**本周值得精读的 2 篇**
- ComVLA：通信-计算协同的 token 剪枝，直接塑造 VLA 边云推理接口。
- LeanWAM：冻结视频先验的紧凑蒸馏，给出 VLA 服务化轻量化与延迟预算的可操作路线。

---
**本次采集**：共采集 2098 条，去重后 1588 条；候选池 120 条，本次精选 9 条。源异常 1 处（见仓库 Actions 日志）。

selected.title: WorldLeague: Benchmarking Physical Agency
selected.summary: AI systems can now operate Blender, follow instructions in complex video games, and manipulate objects with robot arms. What range of physical goals can today's AI systems achieve autonomously? Answering this question requires testing systems on tasks that demand different combinations of perception, memory, planning, and action. We introduce WorldLeague, a benchmark that compares AI systems on a common set of 60 simulated robot tasks by measuring progress toward each task's physical goal from the robot's trajectory. Robots explore scenes to gather evidence in WorldSeek, rearrange objects in WorldShape, and adapt to changes in WorldShift. Tying these goals to a single control interface limits which AI systems can be compared. In WorldLeague, vision-language models (VLMs) choose targets and motions, while vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) use their native controls. For each of six capability dimensions, we measure how much progress a system makes toward its goals (Interactive Score) and how often it achieves them (physical success rate). Together, these measures form the system's Physical Agency Profile. Among 13 representative AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 achieves 13 of the 60 goals and earns the highest mean Interactive Score (28.58/100). Fable leads in four dimensions, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra tie for first on rule-following tasks. Even when VLMs answer every final question correctly, they receive an Interactive Score of zero in 71.8\% of those episodes. WorldLeague gives Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI a shared basis for comparing what AI systems achieve autonomously, from partial progress toward a physical goal to full goal completion. Project Webpage: https://xyangzhou.github.io/WorldLeague

What range of physical goals can today’s AI systems achieve autonomously? Answering this question requires testing systems on tasks that demand different combinations of perception, memory, planning, and action. We introduce WorldLeague , a benchmark that compares AI systems on a common set of 60 simulated robot tasks by measuring progress toward each task’s physical goal from the robot’s trajectory. Robots explore scenes to gather evidence in WorldSeek , rearrange objects in WorldShape , and adapt to changes in WorldShift . Tying these goals to a single control interface limits which AI systems can be compared. In WorldLeague, vision-language models (VLMs) choose targets and motions, while vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) use their native controls. For each of six capability dimensions, we measure how much progress a system makes toward its goals (Interactive Score) and how often it achieves them (physical success rate). Together, these measures form the system’s Physical Agency Profile . Among 13 representative AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 achieves 13 of the 60 goals and earns the highest mean Interactive Score (28.58/100). Fable leads in four dimensions, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra tie for first on rule-following tasks. Even when VLMs answer every final question correctly, they receive an Interactive Score of zero in 71.8% of those episodes. WorldLeague gives Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI a shared basis for comparing what AI systems achieve autonomously, from partial progress toward a physical goal to full goal completion. Figure 1: Example tasks across six dimensions in WorldSeek (blue, right), WorldShape (green, left), and WorldShift (red, below). 1 Introduction Foundation models have recently become a promising direction for building general-purpose robots [ 51 ] . In digital environments, agents built on frontier models can follow instructions in open-world video games [ 4 ] and turn visual references into editable 3D scenes in Blender [ 12 ] . The range of tasks that physical robots can perform has also grown [ 14 , 31 ] . Robots have performed long-horizon household tasks, such as cleaning a kitchen or bedroom, in homes they had never seen during training [ 19 ] . To clean an unfamiliar kitchen, a robot must use what it sees to decide what to do next. Embodied AI systems connect perception to action in different ways [ 16 ] . A vision-language model (VLM) can identify an object from a spatial description [ 7 ] and estimate its distance from other objects [ 5 ] . With a robot interface, it can use such judgments to choose where to move or grasp [ 9 ] . Vision-language-action (VLA) models produce robot actions directly from instructions and visual observations [ 20 ] . For example, Gemini Robotics 1.5 interleaves reasoning and action during multi-step manipulation [ 50 ] . World-action models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions [ 23 , 44 , 57 , 26 ] . This approach has enabled closed-loop manipulation on new tasks and in new environments [ 63 ] . Across these approaches, the ambition is the same. A person specifies a physical goal and leaves the system to decide how to achieve it [ 30 , 9 , 27 , 25 , 39 , 42 ] . We call the system making those decisions the agent and its capacity to choose and execute actions through a body its physical agency . The decisions an agent must make depend on the goal. To find a hidden object, it must decide where to look and what to move out of the way [ 11 , 10 , 17 ] . To put that object through a narrow opening, it must also choose an orientation that fits. An agent may therefore find the right object and still fail to put it away. This leads us to the central question of our study. What range of physical goals can today’s AI systems achieve autonomously? Organizing robot benchmarks around household activities [ 21 , 37 ] obscures what success on each activity establishes about an agent. Consider a robot asked to deliver a cup. If the user names the cup and it is in plain sight, the robot can select it from its current view. If the user asks for the cup that has moved since the robot last visited the room, the robot must use an earlier observation to decide what to pick up. Both tasks count as cup delivery. Yet success on the first leaves the decisive requirement of the second entirely untested. To establish the range of an agent’s physical abilities, we must vary what the agent has to work out for itself and verify that its actions bring about the requested outcome. We introduce WorldLeague , a benchmark of 60 simulated robot tasks organized by the physical demands that determine success. We evaluate VLMs, VLAs, and WAMs against shared goals and constraints. For each task, the robot’s trajectory shows which goal requirements it satisfies and whether it completes the task. The tasks span three tracks, each defined by what the robot must do to achieve its goal. WorldSeek tests navigation and goal grounding as systems explore and gather evidence. WorldShape tests geometric reconfiguration and physical reasoning as systems change the scene. WorldShift tests temporal memory and constraint management as systems track a changing world and recover from disturbances. The three tracks span six capability dimensions (Sec. 3.1 ). We group each task by its primary challenge, and a single task can draw on capabilities from several dimensions. To compare systems across these tasks, we instantiate each goal in a scene with specified objects, initial conditions, and constraints. Physical predicates check conditions such as stable placement or recovery after a disturbance. We inspect all 60 task–scene pairs, verify that reference runs meet the goals and constraints, and check the scoring conditions against the task specifications. Each system pursues its goal through physical interaction. For VLMs, our decision-preserving action abstraction draws on how sensorimotor mechanisms coordinate fine-grained human movement [ 53 , 59 , 13 ] . The interface executes motions, and the agent chooses the targets, action parameters, sequences, and responses to feedback that shape the outcome. We adapt a motion interface [ 9 ] to implement this abstraction on R1 [ 21 ] . VLA and WAM policies use their native interfaces under shared task goals, constraints, and physical scoring rules. We score the resulting trajectory for progress toward individual requirements and for physical success, which requires satisfying the full goal and all task constraints. A Physical Agency Profile reports Interactive Score for progress and physical success rate for complete goal achievement in each capability dimension. For VLMs, terminal question answering (QA) provides an auxiliary measure of scene understanding, outcome recognition, and memory within the same episodes. Among the 13 evaluated embodied AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 earns the highest overall Interactive Score, 28.58 out of 100, and achieves physical success on 13 of its 60 tasks. Fable leads in navigation, goal grounding, geometric reconfiguration, and temporal memory, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra lead in constraint management. The trajectory analysis also identifies goal requirements that remain unmet after systems make physical progress. Of 347 VLM episodes with full terminal QA credit, 249 (71.8%) receive an Interactive Score of zero. These results show that goal-relevant understanding and successful intermediate actions can coexist with unmet physical goals. Turning demonstrated capabilities into desired physical outcomes is central to Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI, which share the ambition of building systems that can pursue human goals through their own actions in the world. WorldLeague turns this ambition into a common experiment. A person specifies the desired outcome, an agent determines how to pursue it through a body, and the evaluation verifies what it achieves in the physical environment. Evaluating systems against common goals and physical success criteria allows advances in perception, reasoning, and control to be assessed in terms of what they enable these systems to accomplish [ 56 ] . Our broader aim is to make autonomous goal achievement a shared measure of progress for AI systems that act in the world. We make three contributions to the evaluation of physical agency in embodied AI systems. • We test physical agency by goal achievement on tasks with different capability combinations. • We build and validate WorldLeague, a suite of 60 tasks that measures progress and physical success across six capability dimensions using shared goals and scoring rules. • We compare the capability profiles of 13 systems and identify goal requirements that remain unmet in episodes with correct answers or partial physical progress. 2 Related Work 2.1 The Demands of Physical Goals BEHAVIOR-1K [ 21 ] takes everyday household activities as the unit of evaluation. Within a single activity, what a robot must decide can change as it acts [ 32 ] . In RoboQuest [ 41 ] , a robot uses trial impressions to decide how to stamp the requested pattern. MeMoREval [ 54 ] makes a later request depend on what the system encountered earlier, while RobotAgentBench [ 34 ] introduces disturbances that require an agent to revise an ongoing manipulation. WorldLeague organizes goals by the primary challenge they pose. Finding a specified object and fitting it through a narrow opening both require identifying the object, but the second goal also requires reasoning about orientation and clearance. Grouping tasks this way lets us trace how success varies across exploration, physical transformation, and adaptation. 2.2 Action Abstraction for Embodied AI Systems An action interface determines which decisions the agent makes [ 62 ] . SayCan [ 1 ] uses a skill’s feasibility to guide selection, and Code as Policies [ 28 ] lets a model compose robot actions in a program. Inner Monologue [ 18 ] feeds execution outcomes back into planning. Show-Harness [ 9 ] translates agent-selected commands through an embodiment-specific interpreter, and HumanCLAW [ 47 ] uses the separation between action selection and motor execution to study how VLMs direct a body. WorldHarness adapts Show-Harness to preserve the VLM’s decisions throughout a task. To place an object, the VLM chooses where to grasp, how far to move, and when to release. The controller executes the motion and returns feedback that the VLM can use to correct its next move. VLA and world-action policies pursue the same goals through their native interfaces. 2.3 Measuring Physical Goal Achievement ESI-Bench [ 15 ] lets systems move and manipulate objects to gather evidence for a spatial answer. ALFRED [ 45 ] scores both task success and the fraction of goal conditions met. IMBench [ 35 ] examines understanding, planning, and execution in separate stages. WorldLeague builds on selected ESI-Bench scene records to pair what a VLM can report with what it physically achieves in the same episode. Once the physical outcome is fixed, terminal QA probes the VLM’s understanding of the scene and its actions. Across all three model families, Physical Agency Profiles show how partial progress and full goal achievement vary across the six dimensions. 2.4 Comparison with Existing Benchmarks Table 1 compares 17 benchmarks by the capabilities their tasks score and the actions their agents control (Appendix A.3 ). RoboQuest and IMBench couple active perception to manipulation by asking agents to uncover information they need to change a physical configuration. MeMoREval tests whether an earlier observation guides a later choice, and RobotAgentBench tests recovery under constraints. WorldLeague evaluates all six dimensions through physical goal achievement, so the same system’s ability to find and manipulate a target can be compared with its ability to track that target as the scene changes. Yanzhe Chen * Zhijun Cao * Zechen Bai * Wenzheng Zeng * Kevin Yuchen Ma Yiqi Lin Guoqiang Liang Xiaokang Liu Ke Sun Kevin Qinghong Lin Mike Zheng Shou † Abstract Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI) , which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench , comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit , a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent’s success rate from 45% to 81% , and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47% . Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback , with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap , where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions. Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability. Figure 1: Robot-use interfaces (RUIs) shape embodied agent performance. Top: RUIKit organizes six action abstractions and two interaction forms into 13 RUIs under shared perception and control. Bottom: (a) Interface choice substantially affects agent success. (b) Decision compression and in-program feedback provide complementary gains. (c) Interface preferences shift from simulation to reality. (d) RUI-specific fine-tuning improves small-model performance in both interaction forms. 1 Introduction Foundation models are moving from understanding the physical world to acting in it [ 74 , 2 , 39 ] . While vision-language-action models learn to predict robot actions [ 7 , 43 , 6 ] , recent agentic systems enable general-purpose models to control robots through tool calls and executable programs [ 52 , 76 , 15 , 27 , 45 , 16 ] . This introduces a critical design choice beyond the model itself: how should an agent interact with a robot? We define the robot-use interface (RUI) as the actions an agent can command and how they are organized for execution. From low-level motion commands [ 3 , 4 ] and image-grounded points [ 25 , 57 ] to semantic skills [ 1 , 37 ] and executable programs [ 52 , 71 ] , the RUI determines what the agent must decide, what can be delegated to execution, and when control returns to the agent. This distinction becomes critical in complex physical tasks. These tasks require agents to gather missing information, react to dynamic events, and correct errors through physical feedback. An interface that demands a new model decision for every small movement can make execution costly and error-prone, while one that provides insufficient feedback may fail when the world deviates from the plan. Thus, reliable execution depends not only on what an agent knows, but also on how decisions and feedback are distributed between the agent and the robot. However, existing embodied benchmarks compare models under fixed interfaces [ 47 , 82 , 18 , 84 , 23 ] , while interface studies typically examine selected design choices [ 27 , 64 , 68 ] . Consequently, the impact of interface design remains poorly understood. In our experiments, changing only the RUI shifts Claude Code’s success rate from 45% to 81%, far exceeding the average performance gap between two frontier agents ( Fig. 1 a). This raises our central question: What makes a good robot-use interface? To answer this question, we introduce RUIBench, a benchmark combining 30 agentic manipulation tasks with a controlled evaluation protocol. These tasks go beyond simple pick-and-place, requiring agents to reason, acquire information through interaction, and adapt to changing physical conditions. They span five suites: world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. The protocol limits agents to RGB-D observations and robot states, keeps the environment evolving during model reasoning, and evaluates task success independently of the agents’ claims. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that disentangles two design choices: action abstraction , which determines what an agent can command, and interaction form , which determines how actions are organized and executed. RUIKit crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms to instantiate 12 interfaces, plus a free-choice interface, all within a shared harness where only the RUI varies ( Fig. 1 ). Across frontier and small models in simulation and 650 real-robot episodes with frontier agents, we find that effective RUIs reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback ( Fig. 1 b), which also makes them easier for small models to learn ( Fig. 1 d). Fine-grained interaction can fragment a clear plan into excessive model decisions, a failure we call execution fragmentation . Composing actions into programs reduces this burden when agents effectively exploit multi-step execution and intermediate feedback. However, real-world execution changes which interfaces are effective, as physical uncertainty demands more opportunities for local correction ( Fig. 1 c). We further uncover a verification gap : agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, while checking individual actions does not guarantee task completion. Together, these findings highlight the importance of allocating decisions, feedback, and verification at appropriate levels. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • Agentic benchmark. We introduce RUIBench with 30 manipulation tasks across five suites and a controlled evaluation protocol for systematically studying RUIs. • Unified framework. We develop RUIKit, spanning 13 interfaces across six action abstractions and two interaction forms under shared perception and control. • Empirical insights. We reveal how decision burden, physical feedback, and task-level verification shape embodied performance across agents and environments. 2 Related Work Figure 2: The 30 tasks of RUIBench. Each row is a suite of six simulated tasks, defined by what success requires: reasoning from prior knowledge, using previously shown visual examples, physical exploration, responding to time-sensitive events, or precise adjustments during contact. The right column shows the task of each suite that also runs on the real robot. Table 1: Comparison with related work. Crossed design evaluates matched action abstractions under per-action and program execution. False claims evaluates completion claims against physical outcomes. Existing systems employ semantic skills and learned-policy tools [ 1 , 37 , 63 , 85 , 48 , 51 , 67 , 83 , 89 , 13 , 61 , 28 ] , executable programs [ 52 , 71 , 76 , 35 , 17 , 40 , 79 ] , spatial constraints and value maps [ 36 , 38 , 60 ] , image-grounded points and paths [ 25 , 57 , 86 , 74 , 50 , 45 , 33 , 88 ] , end-effector poses [ 44 ] , and discrete motion commands [ 3 , 15 , 31 ] . However, these interfaces are typically developed within individual systems, making their independent effects difficult to isolate. Recent studies compare selected action abstractions [ 27 ] , programmatic versus per-action execution [ 64 , 68 , 19 ] , interface families [ 53 , 65 , 4 , 91 ] , harness components [ 80 , 12 , 24 , 73 ] , and planner-policy interfaces [ 34 ] . Yet how these design choices jointly shape agent behavior remains poorly understood. RUIKit addresses this gap by disentangling action abstraction and interaction form , enabling controlled comparisons of their individual and combined effects on agent behavior. Benchmarks for Embodied Foundation Models Existing embodied benchmarks evaluate robot manipulation, generalization, and embodied reasoning [ 47 , 82 , 18 , 49 ] . Recent efforts extend toward foundation-model agents, introducing tasks that demand multi-step reasoning, planning, and physical interaction [ 23 , 84 , 66 , 29 , 46 , 78 , 30 , 14 ] . Evaluation protocols have also become more realistic, incorporating non-privileged observations, continuous physical time, and independent outcome scoring [ 84 , 23 , 65 ] , alongside time and cost considerations [ 26 , 87 , 81 , 41 , 42 ] . However, these benchmarks rarely vary the interface in a controlled way, limiting our understanding of how interface design affects agents facing different interaction demands. Moreover, physical task success does not necessarily imply that an agent correctly recognizes completion. Prior studies investigate visual success detection and failure reasoning [ 21 , 54 , 22 , 90 ] , yet agents can still declare success despite incomplete tasks [ 58 , 84 , 23 ] . RUIBench complements these efforts with 30 agentic tasks spanning five interaction demands and a protocol that separates physical outcomes from agents’ completion claims. Together, RUIBench and RUIKit measure how interface design shapes both execution and completion judgment ( Tab. 1 ). 3 RUIBench RUIBench provides the tasks ( Fig. 2 ) and evaluation protocol ( Sec. 3.2 ) for studying how RUIs shape embodied agent performance. Successful manipulation often requires agents to reason beyond the initial instruction, acquire information through interaction, and adapt to physical feedback. RUIBench captures these demands through 30 tasks in five complementary suites ( Fig. 2 ). World knowledge requires reasoning from prior knowledge, as in the Tower of Hanoi. selected.title: ComVLA: Communication-Aware Split Inference for VLA Models in 6G-Connected Robotics
selected.summary: arXiv:2609.07838v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Connected robotics is an emerging 6G application where mobile robots follow natural-language instructions to manipulate physical objects. The Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that enable this are too large to run on the robot; a common trend is to offload inference to the cloud. The wireless link, however, limits how much sensing data the edge can transmit per control step. Two recent lines address this constraint: semantic communication codecs compress sensor data but require channel-specific retraining, and VLA token pruners select tokens from image but ignore the channel. Our insight is that the dense semantic information contained in the language already indicates which visual tokens matter. We propose ComVLA, a framework that uses this language guidance to adapt the VLA token budget to the channel capacity. Transmitting 32 tokens instead of 512 on the LIBERO benchmark, ComVLA cuts inference compute by 74% and inference latency by 22% versus the original OpenVLA-OFT baseline, at a cost of 1.5 pp in average task success (95.4% vs. 96.9%), and it stays within the capacity budget under Rayleigh and Rician fading. These results demonstrate that co-designing VLA inference and wireless communication is a practical direction for 6G-connected robotics.

Transmitting 32 tokens instead of 512 on the LIBERO benchmark, ComVLA cuts inference compute by 74 % 74\% and inference latency by 22 % 22\% versus the original OpenVLA-OFT baseline, at a cost of 1.5 1.5 pp in average task success ( 95.4 % 95.4\% vs. 96.9 % 96.9\% ), and it stays within the capacity budget under Rayleigh and Rician fading. Index Terms: Robotics, Semantic Communication, Token Prune, 6G Network, Token Communication I Introduction Connected robotics is among the demanding applications envisioned for 6G networks [ 1 ] , requiring low-latency, high-reliability communication between mobile robots and cloud infrastructure. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have driven a paradigm shift in robotics, from traditional perception-planning-control pipelines toward Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. VLAs extend VLMs with an action head, mapping camera observations and natural-language instructions to low-level actions end-to-end. Fig. 1: The motivation of ComVLA. Running full VLA models locally on edge robots is computationally prohibitive, while streaming all visual features to the cloud causes severe bandwidth bottlenecks. ComVLA transmits only the tokens that cross-attention voting identifies as task-critical, reducing both bandwidth and cloud compute. The large VLA parameter scale makes edge deployment impractical, motivating split inference across edge and cloud [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] . However, cloud offloading requires streaming high-dimensional visual features at each control step, which causes severe bandwidth bottlenecks over practical wireless channels. Yet recent findings identify a remedy: visual tokens are highly redundant in large vision-language models, and VLA action decisions depend on a sparse set of task-relevant visual regions [ 5 , 6 ] . Two lines of work exploit this sparsity but each leaves a gap. Semantic communication (SemCom) [ 7 ] addresses the bandwidth mismatch by transmitting task-relevant features rather than raw data, but existing SemCom codecs optimize pixel reconstruction rather than task success and require channel-specific retraining. Beyond SemCom, recent VLA token pruning methods [ 8 ] reduce inference computing by selecting visual tokens via language instructions, but assume a static token budget with no mechanism to adapt to dynamic wireless conditions. In this paper, we propose ComVLA (Communication-aware VLA), a split-inference framework that co-designs semantic token selection with the wireless channel, as illustrated in Fig. 1 . Our key observation is that language instructions naturally identify the task-relevant visual tokens. ComVLA exploits this on the edge and dynamically sets the transmitted token budget to match the instantaneous channel capacity [ 9 ] . The contributions of this paper are: • Framework - A communication-aware VLA inference paradigm. We propose ComVLA, the first split-inference framework for VLA-based robotic manipulation that frames token pruning as an information-theoretically motivated, capacity-constrained token-selection problem, establishing a concrete co-design surface between VLA inference and the wireless link for 6G-connected robotics. • Mechanism - Semantic-guided token selection with a capacity-aligned token budget. We use language instructions to evaluate the task relevance of visual tokens and couple the transmitted token budget directly to the channel capacity, so the payload adapts to the channel in real time. • Results - Robust performance under static and dynamic channels. Transmitting 32 instead of 512 tokens, ComVLA cuts cloud compute by 3.8 × 3.8\times and inference latency by 22 % 22\% at a cost of only 1.5 1.5 pp in task success rate, and maintains robust performance under dynamic fading channels. II Related Work Semantic and Task-Oriented Communication. DeepJSCC [ 10 ] pioneered wireless image transmission, and WITT [ 11 ] later extended it with transformers; a parallel line of task-oriented communication [ 7 ] targets task-level semantic objectives rather than pixel fidelity. These approaches all introduce dedicated codecs that require channel-specific retraining. VLA Models in Edge-Cloud Systems. VLA models demonstrate strong robotic manipulation capabilities but are too large for on-device inference. Such scale motivates split-computing paradigms [ 12 ] that partition inference between edge and cloud, yet existing frameworks still transmit raw visual features over bandwidth-limited channels and treat the link as a fixed pipe. ComVLA co-designs the split-inference token payload with channel capacity. Visual Token Pruning. Visual token pruning methods reduce inference costs but are channel-agnostic. FastV [ 13 ] shows up to half of visual tokens become redundant after the early transformer layers. For VLAs, LightVLA [ 5 ] uses cross-attention on the OpenVLA-OFT backbone, and VLA-ADP [ 8 ] further gates tokens by action dynamics; both, however, target compute reduction and leave the token count blind to channel state [ 14 ] . Cross-attention has become a standard language-conditioned scoring signal across VLA token-pruning methods; ComVLA differs in that the token budget is set by the channel capacity rather than by a fixed compute target. selected.title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming for Robot Foundation Models
selected.summary: arXiv:2611.31715v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper demonstrates an approach for correcting failures of robot foundation models (RFMs) without additional data collection, demonstrations, or training. We apply weight-space programming (WSP), in which a language-model agent directly reads and writes a neural network's parameters, to a large, pre-trained vision-language-action policy. The idea is simple: many policy failures are not random but repeatedly land in the same recognizable stuck state, so if that state is visible in the model's internal activations, a small edit could trigger a corrective movement while leaving the rest of the model's parameters unchanged. A core design choice is where to write the edit: repurposing a few near-silent neurons in the action expert lets the edit switch on in situations associated with the failure and produce a corrective movement, such as lowering the gripper toward the target, that is specified directly rather than learned through training. Empirically, when applied to the pi0.5 policy in simulation, we find that edits to roughly 0.0002% of the parameters can improve success on recurring failures, including for a policy that was already fine-tuned on its task. Reversed and random edits indicate that the gains come from the intended behavior, and the approach works best when the failure situation is recognizable and a simple correction can address it.

selected.title: LeanWAM: Learning Latent World Action Models from Frozen Video Models
selected.summary: arXiv:2611.31740v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World action models (WAMs) typically adapt large pretrained video generators to jointly predict future observations and robot actions, incurring substantial training and deployment costs. Motivated by this finding, we introduce LeanWAM, a latent WAM that transfers video priors from a frozen video generator to a lightweight policy via two-stage training. In the first stage, a Future Extractor compresses observed transitions into 32 predictive tokens. These tokens condition the frozen generator and are jointly shaped by action, RGB, semantic, and geometric supervision, while a compact readout of the generator's hidden states supplies complementary world tokens. The second stage distills both representations into the policy, which learns to predict them from current observations while generating actions. Many WAMs rely on billion-parameter video backbones over dense visual latents [ 2 , 22 , 69 ] . Their representations preserve background, texture, and appearance alongside the robot and object motion needed for control. Modeling all these details increases computation without necessarily improving actions. Compact latent actions [ 65 , 6 ] and compressed perceptual features [ 16 ] offer alternatives, but do not use a pretrained video generator to shape their representations. They therefore do not directly benefit from the motion and interaction priors encoded in these generators, which could complement the supervision available in robot demonstrations. Intermediate frames further improve decoding within the same action horizon and token budget. Together, these findings motivate a compact, action-supervised representation that combines complementary cues across a short clip. We present LeanWAM, a latent world action model that transfers the priors of a frozen pretrained video generator into a lightweight policy. In Stage 1, a Future Extractor compresses a short clip into a predictive code that conditions the frozen video model. The current frame supplies scene context, while the code describes the transition. Semantic, geometric, and RGB supervision at increasing depths guides this description without additional generation branches. selected.summary: arXiv:2611.33010v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can a simple mirror expose the limitations of today's robotic manipulation policies? Inspired by the mirror self-recognition test in animal cognition, we investigate whether robot policies can reliably manipulate physical objects in scenes containing their reflections. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark built on RoboDojo that preserves task objectives, success criteria, and policy checkpoints while comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, every mirror condition reduces aggregate success rates: averaged over the three conditions, the drop ranges from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies, and it reaches 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Trajectory and contact analyses instead reveal recurring behaviors consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. The classical mirror self-recognition test examines whether animals can use reflections to guide actions toward their own bodies [ 10 ] . Inspired by this behavioral probe, we ask whether robot policies can reliably locate and manipulate physical objects when their observations also contain reflections of those objects. Mirrors create a structured discrepancy between visual appearance and actionable space. Reflections preserve recognizable features and change with physical objects, yet their apparent locations contain no additional manipulable targets. They can also adjoin real objects in images, forming composite contours, or reveal otherwise occluded targets. These properties enable tests of two complementary capabilities: maintaining reliable manipulation in the presence of reflections, and using reflected observations to act on occluded targets. Recent advances in generalist robot policies have expanded the range of manipulation tasks that can be performed from visual and language inputs, yet whether these policies possess the two capabilities above remains unclear. Vision-Language-Action models directly generate actions from multimodal observations, while World Action Models jointly model actions and future observations [ 2 , 29 ] . Agentic policies provide another approach by selecting and invoking robot tools through repeated observation and reasoning [ 15 ] . However, strong performance under standard evaluation conditions does not establish robustness to changes in visual evidence. Controlled perturbation benchmarks have demonstrated substantial performance degradation under variations in viewpoints, lighting, backgrounds, and other conditions [ 7 ] . Reflections are not covered by these perturbations: rather than altering appearance, they duplicate task-relevant content at locations with a known geometric relationship to the physical scene. Existing mirror-based evaluations have begun to examine embodied agents’ self-centric perception and interaction, including tasks inspired by mirror self-recognition [ 12 ] . We investigate a different operational setting: generalist policies performing external-object manipulation under controlled mirror configurations. The question posed above breaks down into three parts: how reflections affect task completion, whether observed degradation extends beyond the effects of an inserted physical panel, and what execution behaviors accompany these changes. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, an evaluation benchmark built on RoboDojo [ 3 ] . As illustrated in Fig. , it preserves the original manipulation objectives and success criteria while evaluating policies under four conditions: no mirror, a single mirror, dual mirrors, and a mirrored tabletop. On a shared set of eight tasks, we pair layouts and policy seeds across conditions to measure changes relative to each policy’s own mirror-free baseline. For selected policies, geometrically matched non-reflective panels provide additional controls for the effects of inserting physical structures. We further design three diagnostic scenarios, namely grasping on a mirrored tabletop, pushing an object connected to its reflection, and acting with reflections as the main visual cue, combining task outcomes with trajectory and contact observations. This protocol enables researchers to assess reflection robustness using existing policies and task evaluators, and to characterize failures beyond aggregate success rates. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, all three mirror conditions reduce aggregate success rates, with average drops of 10.8–56.7 percentage points across policies. Matched panel comparisons show that 50–88% of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robot–panel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. The accompanying behaviors are consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. The three diagnostics further show more frequent empty grasps, pushing progress that varies with policy and contour, and limited physical-target contact even with mirror-related hints. Real-robot experiments with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and FastWAM show a similar overall degradation trend. Together, these results reveal a shared vulnerability to reflections across diverse robot policies. 2 Related Work 2.1 Robotic Manipulation Benchmarks and Visual Robustness Robotic manipulation benchmarks provide complementary tools for evaluating policy capabilities. LIBERO studies knowledge transfer in lifelong robot learning [ 20 ] . RoboTwin 2.0 combines scalable data generation with structured domain randomization for bimanual manipulation [ 4 ] , while RoboDojo provides a unified simulation and real-world evaluation framework for generalist manipulation policies [ 3 ] . Recent benchmarks place greater emphasis on robustness beyond nominal task success. LIBERO-Plus introduces controlled perturbations to object layouts, camera viewpoints, robot initial states, language, lighting, backgrounds, and sensor observations [ 7 ] . LIBERO-VPro evaluates closed-loop visual robustness by perturbing the evidence available during execution, including observation degradation, camera staleness, and cross-view consistency [ 17 ] . LIBERO-Pro2.0 further covers static and runtime shifts across environmental, observational, execution, robot-state, and language dimensions [ 35 ] . RoboPRO complements success-based evaluation with collision metrics under clutter and controlled perturbations [ 18 ] . Building on these evaluation principles, our work focuses on mirror-augmented manipulation, where reflections introduce structured visual ambiguity alongside physical scene changes. We evaluate task outcomes and contact behavior, and use geometrically matched non-reflective panels to examine performance differences beyond the presence of the panel itself. 2.2 Mirror Perception and Spatial Reasoning Mirrors challenge visual understanding because reflected objects can resemble directly observed objects while occupying different physical locations. Early mirror-detection methods identify reflective regions through contextual contrasts [ 28 ] , while video-based approaches exploit spatial and temporal correspondences [ 19 ] . These methods address the localization of mirror regions rather than the action consequences of reflected observations. Mirror3D further estimates mirror geometry to refine unreliable depth measurements on reflective surfaces [ 26 ] . More recently, MIRA-Bench evaluates reflection-aware perception, spatial reasoning, and scene-level decisions in real RGB-D mirror scenes, exposing difficulties in reconciling reflected appearance with depth measurements [ 30 ] . MirrorQA examines subject-centered left–right reasoning in mirror contexts [ 21 ] . Related diagnostic benchmarks, including HallusionBench [ 11 ] and IllusionVQA [ 25 ] , investigate visual illusions and failures of image-grounded reasoning. Unlike these perception-focused studies, we evaluate task outcomes and contact behavior during closed-loop manipulation under reflections. 2.3 Mirror-Mediated Robotic Interaction Robotic mirror research spans geometry and sensorimotor learning. Hart and Scassellati infer mirror viewpoints from learned sensorimotor relationships [ 14 ] . Marchand and Chaumette develop visual servoing for robot-mounted mirrors [ 22 ] , while Lanillos et al. combine active inference and sensorimotor prediction for mirror self-recognition and self/other distinction [ 16 ] . Yoshioka et al. exploit mirror reflections to observe occluded regions, while UMI incorporates side mirrors for manipulation and shows that corrected mirror views can outperform uncorrected ones [ 31 , 6 ] . Recent embodied evaluations extend mirror-based tests to multimodal agents. MirrorBench studies self-centric intelligence through simulated mirror interaction [ 12 ] , while Ziliotto et al. evaluate whether agents can infer hidden self-attributes from reflections and use this evidence to guide actions [ 36 ] . Beyond self-centric tasks, Being-M0.7 evaluates mirror-assisted grasping of a directly occluded toy in a real-world humanoid task [ 33 ] . Our work studies reflection robustness across multiple generalist policies and manipulation tasks under controlled mirror configurations. 3 Benchmark Design and Evaluation Protocol Built on RoboDojo [ 3 ] , RoboDojo-Mirror evaluates policy robustness to reflections while preserving the original task objectives and success criteria. Fig. 2 summarizes the paired evaluation protocol and controls. 3.1 Policy and Task Selection We evaluate five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies: WALL-OSS-1.0-Lite (WALL-OSS) [ 27 ] , VPP2 [ 13 ] , Awomo-0.5 [ 1 ] , Rex-M1 Preview [ 9 ] , and GPT-6-Astra (Astra) [ 34 , 23 ] . This selection covers different approaches to generating robot actions from visual observations. For open-weight policies, we use official checkpoints and inference configurations. Within each policy, we hold the checkpoint, observation interface, action interface, and inference settings fixed across scene conditions. For Astra, the available camera streams, robot-state interface, motion tools, and inference budget are likewise held fixed across conditions. We select a shared eight-task set 𝒯 \mathcal{T} that balances diverse manipulation requirements with strong overall RoboDojo leaderboard performance. selected.summary: ## Purpose Last split (6/6) of Kimi K3.1: sparse MLA optimizations for decode context parallelism (DCP). Splits 1-5 are merged (#66030, #66028, #66037, #66532, #65685), so this diff is only the DCP part. Nothing here changes behavior without DCP. Changes: - **CuTe DSL direct A2A LSE reduce (SM100).** Same buffers and signal protocol as the CUDA op, 2 launches instead of 4. - **DCP ShardQ.** Extends the TP ShardQ from #63956 to DCP == TP (FlashInfer sparse MLA, SM100). Each rank pushes its KV shard of the step's prefill requests (MLA and indexer pages) into a symmetric-memory workspace (`vllm/v1/attention/ops/dcp_shardq`), then handles a slice of the prefill tokens with all heads over the gathered context. Prefill tokens skip the query all-gather, LSE combine and top-k merge; decode tokens stay on the DCP path. The workspace holds `max_model_len` tokens (plus one page per request). A step that doesn't fit runs on the DCP path as on `main`; no scheduler changes. Controlled by `attention_config.sparse_mla_shard_q` (on by default, same as TP ShardQ); needs an fp8 indexer K cache. - **nvfp4_ds_mla + DCP** is now accepted; its chunked-context gather reads the local context. - **FlashMLA sparse:** DCP can gather up to 128 query heads, and long fp8 mixed batches run in chunks. - The indexer metadata no longer syncs to read DCP-local lengths back from the GPU. - Kimi K3.1 DSA layer hooks for DCP ShardQ. Related: #65555 is the ROCm DSv4.1 ShardQ indexer. ## Test Plan / Results ### End-to-end TTFT at 108k tokens All three configurations used the official `moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro` checkpoint (`d9e99b0792a5`) on the same eight B300 GPUs with TP8/DCP8. We sent one streaming request at a time. After one warmup, each configuration processed the same three prompts three times each. The per-prompt columns show the median of three requests.
